label: Intrinsic randomness generation explains most randomness in nature
statement: The mechanism in which a system's own deterministic rules generate randomness without any random input is ultimately responsible for a large fraction, and perhaps essentially all, of the randomness seen in the natural world.
quote: I believe that this mechanism is in fact ultimately responsible for a large fraction, if not essentially all, of the randomness that we see in the natural world.
scope: random-looking phenomena in the natural world

label: Hardware noise-based random generators deviate from perfect randomness
statement: Devices that generate randomness by amplifying microscopic environmental noise (spark gaps, vacuum tubes, semiconductor diodes) have consistently been found to produce output with significant deviations from perfect randomness, because the sampling device relaxes only gradually and because the environment itself has correlations.
quote: But despite such sensitivity to microscopic effects, what has consistently been found in practice is that the output from such devices has significant deviations from perfect randomness.
scope: physical random number generators based on electronic or other environmental noise

label: Sensitive dependence alone does not make behavior random
statement: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions, as in chaos theory, does not by itself make a system behave randomly; it only makes ever-less-significant digits of the initial conditions matter, so the behavior is random only if those digit sequences are random, and there is no reason to assume the numbers occurring in nature have random digits.
quote: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions thus does not in and of itself imply that a system will behave in a random way.
scope: chaotic dynamical systems such as the doubling (shift) map

label: Randomness from initial conditions lasts only a limited number of steps
statement: In physical chaotic systems such as kneading, mirror arrangements or pegboards, randomness can be attributed purely to initial conditions only for a small number of steps (around ten collisions for a pegboard), because amplification quickly reaches atomic scales and environmental perturbations take over; the limit is set by the separation between observed large-scale and uncontrollable small-scale features.
quote: So the idea that randomness comes purely from initial conditions can be realistic only for a fairly small number of steps; randomness which is seen after that must therefore typically be attributed to other mechanisms.
scope: physical systems with sensitive dependence on initial conditions

label: Solar system motion should show sensitive dependence over millions of years
statement: Although planetary motion looks regular on human timescales, sensitive dependence on initial conditions should ultimately occur in the solar system, producing significant randomness over a few million years that may explain some present-day features of the solar system.
quote: But calculations imply that sensitive dependence on initial conditions should ultimately occur even in our solar system.
scope: orbital dynamics of planets and other bodies in the solar system

label: Rule 30 center column passes all practical tests of randomness
statement: The sequence of center-cell colors produced by the rule 30 cellular automaton from a single black cell shows no regularities under any standard statistical, mathematical or perceptual method of analysis, making it at least as random as any phenomenon in nature that is considered random.
quote: But the remarkable fact is that none of these methods seem to reveal any real regularities whatsoever in the rule 30 cellular automaton sequence.
scope: the center column of the rule 30 elementary cellular automaton

label: Maximal-period linear congruential generators still show strong nonrandomness
statement: Linear congruential random number generators designed to have maximal repetition period have repeatedly turned out to deviate substantially from perfect randomness (for example, successive outputs plotted as points fall on regular stripes), because the mathematical tractability that guarantees their period also implies regularity.
quote: But in practice over the years, one after another linear congruential generator that has been constructed to have maximal repetition period has turned out to exhibit very substantial deviations from perfect randomness.
scope: linear congruential pseudorandom number generators

label: Amenability to mathematical analysis implies deviations from randomness
statement: The very possibility of detailed mathematical analysis of a system tends to imply that its output has at least some deviations from perfect randomness, whereas simple rules not constrained by the need for such analysis can generate highly random behavior.
quote: the very possibility of any detailed mathematical analysis tends to imply the presence of at least some deviations from perfect randomness.
scope: deterministic systems used to generate randomness, including pseudorandom generators

label: Rapid production of much randomness indicates intrinsic generation
statement: Whenever a large amount of randomness is produced in a short time, intrinsic randomness generation is overwhelmingly likely to be responsible, because it uses every component of a system to produce new randomness and has no length limit, whereas environmental amplification is slow and initial-condition randomness is short-lived.
quote: The basic answer, I believe, is that whenever a large amount of randomness is produced in a short time, intrinsic randomness generation is overwhelmingly likely to be the mechanism responsible.
scope: natural and engineered systems that produce randomness

label: Intrinsically generated randomness is repeatable across experimental runs
statement: If randomness in an experiment comes from intrinsic generation, then even the precise details of the random-looking behavior should be repeatable from one run to the next, because such behavior is robust to perturbations below a critical size, whereas randomness from the environment or from initial conditions should show little or no repeatability.
quote: But what is remarkable is that if intrinsic randomness generation is the mechanism at work, then the precise details of the behavior can also be repeatable.
scope: carefully controlled experiments showing random-looking behavior

label: Detailed visual similarities in organisms imply intrinsic randomness
statement: Detailed visual similarities between members of the same species, and between the two symmetric sides of a system, in features that look complex and random cannot be attributed to environmental or initial-condition randomness and must come from intrinsic randomness generation.
quote: And instead, there is no choice but to conclude that the randomness must in fact come from the mechanism of intrinsic randomness generation that I have discovered in simple programs, and discussed in this section.
scope: complex-looking patterns in physical, biological and other systems, especially bilaterally symmetric ones

label: Randomness lets discrete components produce continuous behavior
statement: Systems made of discrete components appear smooth and continuous on large scales mainly because microscopic randomness averages out the discreteness, and it does not matter whether that randomness comes from outside or from intrinsic generation, as shown by random walks, aggregation models and deterministic cellular automata that grow circular shapes.
quote: But it turns out that all that really seems to matter is that randomness is present: the mechanism through which it arises appears to be largely irrelevant.
scope: discrete systems such as random walks, aggregation models and cellular automata, and fluids made of molecules

label: Continuity requires slow features relative to small-scale random changes
statement: Continuous large-scale behavior can arise in a system with discrete components only when there are features that evolve slowly relative to the rate of small-scale random changes; for growth, the random small-scale changes must occur much faster than the overall growth.
quote: In general the point is that continuous behavior can arise in systems with discrete components only when there are features that evolve slowly relative to the rate of small-scale random changes.
scope: discrete systems with randomness, including growth processes and domain coarsening

label: Density-driven discrete transitions are rare in 1D CAs, common in higher dimensions
statement: Cellular automata in which a continuous change in initial density of black cells produces a discrete switch in long-time behavior, with whichever color was initially more common taking over the whole system, are fairly rare in one dimension, where domain boundaries often get stuck, but become increasingly common in two and more dimensions.
quote: And so long as the boundaries of the regions do not get stuck—as happens in many one-dimensional cellular automata—the result is that whichever color was initially more common eventually takes over the whole system.
scope: cellular automata in one, two and more dimensions started from random initial conditions of varying density

label: Continuous rules can yield discrete behavior, so discrete models often fit
statement: Even systems governed by continuous equations, such as certain chemical reaction kinetics, commonly have a limited number of stable states with discrete transitions between them, and because discrete overall behavior is often a system's most obvious feature, discrete models like cellular automata are often the most appropriate.
quote: And in fact it is quite common for such behavior to be one of the most obvious features of a system—which is why discrete systems like cellular automata end up often being the most appropriate models.
scope: natural systems with continuous underlying dynamics but discrete overall behavior, such as phase transitions and bistable chemical reactions

label: Complex natural behavior is almost never best explained by constraints
statement: Almost none of the complex behavior seen in nature is best explained as the satisfaction of constraints, because finding a pattern that satisfies a constraint is usually far too difficult a computation to happen routinely in nature; explicit processes of evolution are the more plausible explanation.
quote: But despite this, my strong suspicion is that of all the examples of complex behavior that we see in nature almost none can in the end best be explained in terms of constraints.
scope: complex behavior in physical and other natural systems

label: Local-improvement procedures get stuck when satisfying discrete constraints
statement: For discrete constraint systems the landscape of constraint violations is almost always jagged, so iterative procedures that only move downhill almost invariably get stuck far from a solution, random modifications help only slowly, and no speed-up techniques work well across broad classes of systems; hence natural systems are unlikely to come close to satisfying such constraints.
quote: So what this suggests is that even if in some idealized sense a system in nature might be expected to satisfy certain constraints, it is likely that in practice the system will actually not have a way to come even close to doing this.
scope: iterative and annealing-like procedures for discrete constraint satisfaction, and natural systems assumed to satisfy constraints

label: Pushed or jiggled spheres do not reach densest packing
statement: Unlike identical coins in two dimensions, which readily form the densest hexagonal packing when pushed together, balls in three dimensions pushed together or jiggled almost always get stuck and essentially never reach the densest repetitive packing, which seems obtainable only by careful one-by-one placement.
quote: But if one just tries pushing balls together they almost always get stuck, and never take on anything like the arrangement shown.
scope: packing of identical spheres and circles under physical compression or agitation

label: Complex biological forms come from growth rules, not selection-driven constraints
statement: Natural selection can produce forms determined by constraint satisfaction only when those forms are rather simple; complex biological forms are associated instead with explicit evolution rules, mostly those governing the growth of an individual organism.
quote: when more complex forms are seen they once again tend to be associated not with constraints but rather with the effects of explicit evolution rules—mostly those governing the growth of an individual organism.
scope: biological forms shaped by natural selection and development

label: Rule complexity does not determine behavioral complexity
statement: There is no direct correspondence between the complexity of a system's underlying rules and the complexity of its behavior: some of the simplest rules yield highly complex behavior, fairly complicated rules often yield simple behavior, and rules differing at a single position can behave very differently.
quote: Traditional intuition might have made one assume that there must be a direct correspondence between the complexity of observed behavior and the complexity of underlying rules. But one of the central discoveries of this book is that in fact there is not.
scope: simple programs such as cellular automata, and by extension natural systems

label: Nesting in nature mostly arises from building up, not splitting down
statement: Nested patterns can arise either from elements splitting or branching into smaller ones or from larger elements being built up from smaller ones (as in additive cellular automata), and the building-up route is probably the more common origin of nesting in nature.
quote: it can also arise when larger elements are built up from smaller ones—and indeed I suspect that this is its more common origin in nature.
scope: nested (self-similar) patterns in natural systems

label: Merging of independently growing domains generically produces nesting
statement: Nesting can arise from random initial conditions through progressive annihilation of randomly placed elements: in essentially any system where domains grow fairly independently and then progressively merge, an overall nested pattern resembling a river-tributary tree forms, even when domain boundaries move as random walks.
quote: And indeed in essentially any system where there are domains that grow fairly independently and then progressively merge the same basic overall nesting will be seen.
scope: cellular automata such as rules 184 and 110 and other domain-coarsening systems from random initial conditions

label: Models of complex systems should first be judged by comparing overall pictures
statement: For systems with complex behavior, a model cannot be adequately assessed by matching a few extracted numbers; the best first test is a visual comparison of the model's overall behavior with that of the real system.
quote: by far the best first step in assessing a model is not to look at numbers or other details, but rather just to use one's eyes, and to compare overall pictures of a system with pictures from the model.
scope: scientific modelling of systems with complex behavior

label: Snowflake shapes arise from growth inhibition captured by a hexagonal cellular automaton
statement: The main features of snowflake shapes are reproduced by a hexagonal cellular automaton in which a cell becomes ice only if exactly one neighbor is ice, which represents the inhibition of nearby growth by released latent heat.
quote: One can capture this basic effect by having a cellular automaton with rules in which cells become black if they have exactly one black neighbor, but stay white whenever they have more than one black neighbor.
scope: growth of snowflakes (ice crystals from water vapor)

label: Growing snowflakes should alternate between tree-like and faceted shapes
statement: During the growth of an individual snowflake its shape should alternate between tree-like and faceted forms, as new branches grow and then collide with one another.
quote: one expects that during the growth of a particular snowflake there should be alternation between tree-like and faceted shapes, as new branches grow but then collide with each other.
scope: time course of individual snowflake growth

label: Randomness in crystal shapes is often intrinsically generated by simple growth rules
statement: Apparent randomness in the shapes of crystalline materials often arises intrinsically from simple deterministic growth rules, rather than from randomness in the seed or the growth environment.
quote: And contrary to what has always been assumed, I suspect that this is actually how the apparent randomness that one sometimes sees in shapes formed by crystalline materials often comes about.
scope: growth shapes of crystals

label: Randomness of fracture surfaces comes from a material-independent intrinsic mechanism
statement: The roughness and randomness of fracture paths does not come from random irregularities in a material but from a general mechanism in which deterministic interactions of element displacements around a moving crack intrinsically generate randomness, as in a simple cellular automaton model.
quote: I nevertheless suspect that even when much more realistic models for specific materials are used, the fundamental mechanisms responsible for randomness will still be very much the same as in the extremely simple model shown here.
scope: fracture of solids, from single crystals to geological faults

label: Conservation plus microscopic randomness yields universal fluid behavior
statement: Any system of particles that conserves quantities such as particle number and momentum and has sufficient microscopic randomness will show the same large-scale fluid behavior, so a discrete cellular automaton particle model can reproduce the flow of real fluids.
quote: so long as certain physical quantities such as particle number and momentum are conserved, then whenever there is sufficient microscopic randomness, it is almost inevitable that the same overall fluid behavior will be obtained.
scope: fluids and discrete lattice-gas models of fluids

label: Large-scale fluid flow shows little sensitive dependence on initial conditions
statement: In almost all cases, large-scale fluid behavior does not depend discernibly on the detailed initial conditions; small perturbations are damped out by viscosity, so sensitive dependence (chaos) is the exception rather than the rule.
quote: when it comes to large-scale fluid behavior, it seems to be true that in almost all cases there is no discernible difference between what happens with different detailed initial conditions.
scope: large-scale behavior of real and model fluid flows, including turbulence

label: Turbulent randomness is intrinsically generated at the level of large-scale fluid motion
statement: The randomness seen in turbulent fluids is mostly neither inserted from outside nor inherited from molecular randomness, but is intrinsically generated by the dynamics of the large-scale fluid motion itself.
quote: Instead, what seems to be happening is that intrinsic randomness generation occurs directly at the level of large-scale fluid motion.
scope: turbulent fluid flow

label: Random-looking yet repeatable fluid flows should be producible
statement: Because turbulent randomness is generated intrinsically by large-scale motion, carefully prepared experiments should produce fluid flows that look random yet are essentially the same on every repeated run.
quote: with sufficiently careful preparation it should be possible to produce patterns of flow that seem quite random but that are nevertheless effectively repeatable—so that they look essentially the same on every successive run of an experiment.
scope: laboratory fluid flows at turbulent or near-turbulent conditions

label: Most biological complexity comes from randomly chosen programs, not natural selection
statement: Most of the complexity seen in biological organisms originates from the abstract fact that many randomly chosen programs produce complex behavior, rather than from adaptation or careful optimization by natural selection.
quote: the vast majority of the complexity we see in biological systems actually has its origin in the purely abstract fact that among randomly chosen programs many give rise to complex behavior.
scope: complex forms and patterns in biological organisms

label: Evolution cannot have found optimal solutions to complex fitness constraints
statement: Since iterative random search converges only for simple constraints, the roughly trillion generations of life on Earth are insufficient to find optimal solutions to complex constraints, so most features of organisms are merely good-enough solutions rather than optima.
quote: it is still completely implausible that the trillion or so generations of organisms since the beginning of life on Earth would be sufficient to allow optimal solutions to be found to constraints of any significant complexity.
scope: biological evolution as an iterative random search

label: Complexity of individual organism parts has been roughly constant for eons
statement: The complexity of individual parts of organisms, such as textures and other morphological features, was already present in early fossils and has not changed much in at least several hundred million years.
quote: there is every indication that the level of complexity of individual parts of organisms has not changed much in at least several hundred million years.
scope: fossil record of morphological complexity

label: Features that change fastest between species are the most complex
statement: Among related species, the features that differ most rapidly (such as pigmentation and texture patterns) are the ones that show the most obvious complexity, while features under natural selection stay nearly constant.
quote: it is almost always those features which change most rapidly between species that show the most obvious signs of complexity.
scope: variation of traits among closely related species

label: Genetic programs for complex pigment patterns are short
statement: The genetic programs that generate patterns such as those on mollusc shells are short, as indicated by the large variety of patterns within species, and molecular biology should be able to isolate them and confirm their brevity.
quote: Modern molecular biology should soon be able to isolate the specific programs responsible, say, for the patterns on mollusc shells, and see explicitly how long they are. But there are already indications that these programs are quite short.
scope: genetic control of pigmentation patterns, especially on mollusc shells

label: Natural selection works meaningfully only on simple behavior
statement: The power of natural selection is limited: it can systematically optimize only systems or parts of systems whose behavior is simple, and achieves very little when behavior is complex.
quote: what I suspect is that in the end natural selection can only operate in a meaningful way on systems or parts of systems whose behavior is in some sense quite simple.
scope: natural selection acting on biological traits

label: Natural selection makes organisms simpler and more engineering-like
statement: Rather than generating complexity, the main effect of natural selection is to make biological systems avoid complexity, favoring simple, somewhat independent components with smoothly adjustable properties, as in engineered systems.
quote: my strong suspicion is that in fact the main effect of natural selection is almost exactly the opposite: it tends to make biological systems avoid complexity, and be more like systems in engineering.
scope: biological organisms under natural selection

label: Convergent structures recur because they are common among programs, not optimal
statement: When similar complex structures arise independently in very different organisms, this is because those structures are common outputs of programs of certain kinds, not because they are optimal.
quote: the reason certain structures appear repeatedly is just that they are somehow common among programs of certain kinds
scope: convergent evolution

label: Natural selection does not inherently drive organisms toward more elaborate structure
statement: Natural selection does not inevitably produce progressively more elaborate organisms; increases in complexity in the fossil record come from random mutations that add features without fatal flaws, while selection's systematic effect is to simplify.
quote: It is certainly not the case—as is often assumed—that natural selection somehow inevitably leads to organisms with progressively more elaborate structures and progressively larger numbers of parts.
scope: long-term trends in organismal complexity

label: Plant branching patterns come from simple substitution-system growth rules
statement: The overall branching patterns of plants, from algae to ferns to trees and flowering plants, are produced by simple growth rules in which each stem tip repeatedly splits into smaller copies of itself at fixed relative lengths and angles.
quote: And no doubt it is from such simple rules of growth that most such overall branching patterns come.
scope: overall branching architecture of plants

label: Leaf shapes arise from the same simple branching process as whole plants
statement: The shapes of leaves, from smooth to prickly to irregular, are produced by the same simple branching growth process that governs overall plant forms, and small changes in its parameters can change leaf shape greatly.
quote: I strongly suspect that in fact the very same simple process of branching is ultimately responsible both for the overall forms of plants, and for the shapes of their leaves.
scope: leaf shape development in plants

label: The 137.5° phyllotaxis angle results from a simple inhibition growth process
statement: The near-universal 137.5° (golden-ratio) angle between successive plant organs is not an optimization found by natural selection but the inevitable result of a simple process where each new element forms where a chemical concentration is highest and depletes it nearby.
quote: And instead what I strongly suspect is that the patterns are just inevitable consequences of a rather simple process of growth not unlike one that was already discussed, at least in general terms, nearly a century ago.
scope: phyllotaxis and spiral arrangements of plant organs

label: Simple growth-rate models generate essentially all mollusc shell shapes
statement: Mollusc shell shapes result from secreting material at different rates around the shell opening, and essentially every form produced by a simple growth model with a few parameters is found in some real mollusc.
quote: The remarkable fact illustrated on the next page is that essentially all of them are found in some kind of mollusc or another.
scope: coiled shell shapes of molluscs

label: Animal embryos develop hierarchically because of a fixed length scale
statement: Because regions of tissue a few tenths of a millimeter across subdivide into regions using different sections of the genetic program (controlled by chemical gradients and homeobox genes), embryos necessarily develop hierarchically, e.g. a leg region before a foot region.
quote: The existence of a fixed length scale at which such processes occur then almost inevitably implies that an embryo must develop in a somewhat hierarchical fashion.
scope: embryonic development of animals

label: Shape differences between related animals come from differing growth rates
statement: Differences in shape among related animals are largely due to different patterns of relative growth rates of their parts, so their shapes are related by simple smooth geometric transformations.
quote: differences between the shapes and forms of animals may often be due in large part merely to different patterns in the rates of growth for their different parts.
scope: body shapes of animals within a family or order

label: Diversity of plant and animal forms comes from different simple rules
statement: Most of the diversity and complexity in the forms of plants and animals arises because slightly different, essentially randomly picked simple growth rules lead to very different and often complex behavior.
quote: it is this basic phenomenon that I suspect is responsible for most of the diversity and complexity that we see in the forms of plants and animals.
scope: forms of plants and animals

label: Mollusc shell pigment patterns are generated like one-dimensional cellular automata
statement: Pigmentation patterns on mollusc shells are produced line by line by pigment-secreting elements whose new states depend on neighbors' previous states, so the range of shell patterns closely matches the patterns of the simplest symmetric one-dimensional cellular automata.
quote: comparing the patterns in these pictures with patterns on actual mollusc shells, one notices the remarkable fact that the range of patterns that occur in the two cases is extremely similar.
scope: pigmentation patterns on mollusc shells

label: Mollusc shell pattern rules are effectively random, not optimized
statement: The rules generating mollusc shell patterns are effectively chosen at random from the simplest possibilities rather than optimized against predators or for mates, as shown by many species whose patterns are hidden by opaque skin throughout life.
quote: these patterns are instead generated by rules that are in effect chosen at random from among a collection of the simplest possibilities.
scope: evolution of mollusc shell pigmentation

label: Animal coat patterns arise from local activation and longer-range inhibition rules
statement: The few recurring kinds of animal pigmentation patterns (spots, labyrinths, stripes) are produced by a simple rule in which each element tends to match the average color of nearby elements and oppose that of elements further away, as in a two-dimensional cellular automaton.
quote: The idea is that when a pattern forms, the color of each element will tend to be the same as the average color of nearby elements, and opposite to the average color of elements further away.
scope: pigmentation patterns on animal skins and coats

label: Short-timescale market randomness comes from internal market dynamics
statement: Much of the apparent randomness in financial prices, especially on timescales of minutes or seconds, is generated by the internal dynamics of trading entities interacting with one another, not by external news or changes in the value of the asset.
quote: particularly on short timescales much of the randomness that one sees is purely a consequence of internal dynamics in the market, and has little if anything to do with the nature or value of what is being traded.
scope: price fluctuations in financial markets

label: Simple cellular automaton markets generate random-looking price series
statement: In a market modelled as a one-dimensional cellular automaton of buy/sell agents reacting to neighbors, any rule that lets information eventually propagate to all agents makes the running buy-minus-sell total show significant randomness.
quote: as soon as the underlying rule for the cellular automaton is such that information will eventually propagate from one entity to all others—in effect a minimal version of an efficient market hypothesis—it is essentially inevitable that running totals of numbers of cells will exhibit significant randomness.
scope: one-dimensional cellular automaton models of markets

label: Reversible rules are rare among cellular automata
statement: Reversibility is rare among simple cellular automaton rules: only 6 of the 256 elementary two-color nearest-neighbor rules are reversible, and only 1800 of the 7,625,597,484,987 three-color nearest-neighbor rules are.
quote: There are a total of 7,625,597,484,987 cellular automata with three colors and nearest-neighbor rules, and searching through these one finds just 1800 that are reversible.
scope: one-dimensional cellular automata with two and three colors and nearest-neighbor rules

label: Reversible systems can behave as complexly as any other
statement: Although only a tiny fraction of possible rules are reversible, reversible cellular automata can still produce behavior, including apparent randomness and localized structures, as complex as that of non-reversible systems.
quote: So in the end it seems that even though only a very small fraction of possible systems have the property of being reversible, such systems can still exhibit behavior just as complex as one sees anywhere else.
scope: reversible cellular automata, including second-order rules constructed to be time-reversal symmetric

label: Second Law holds because experiments cannot prepare randomness-decreasing states
statement: The Second Law of Thermodynamics is observed to hold because practical experiments can only set up initial conditions that are simple to describe and construct, and finding initial conditions of a reversible system that would lead to decreasing randomness requires computation as great as the system's own evolution.
quote: The consequence of this is that no reasonable experiment can ever involve setting up the kind of initial conditions that will lead to decreases in randomness, and that therefore all practical experiments will tend to show only increases in randomness.
scope: reversible physical systems and the experiments performed on them; origin of the Second Law of Thermodynamics

label: Reversible rule 37R does not obey the Second Law
statement: The reversible cellular automaton rule 37R, even as a closed system, shows neither a systematic trend toward increasing randomness nor simple predictable behavior, but fluctuates indefinitely between more and less ordered states, so it does not obey the Second Law for practical purposes.
quote: There is, I believe, no choice but to conclude that for practical purposes rule 37R simply does not obey the Second Law.
scope: the second-order reversible elementary cellular automaton rule 37R in finite closed regions

label: The Second Law is general but not universally valid
statement: The Second Law of Thermodynamics is an important and general principle but is not universally valid; many systems in nature behave like rule 37R and do not show a uniform trend toward increasing randomness.
quote: And indeed I strongly suspect that there are many systems in nature which behave in more or less the same way. The Second Law is an important and quite general principle—but it is not universally valid.
scope: physical, biological and other natural systems to which the Second Law is applied

label: Biological order arises from partitioning into separated compartments
statement: Biological systems can show increasing order despite the Second Law mainly because they partition into parts (cells, organisms) separated by membrane-like boundaries, within which organized behavior can occur while the boundary survives.
quote: This basic mechanism may well be the main one at work in many biological systems: each cell or each organism becomes separated from others, and while it survives, it can exhibit organized behavior.
scope: biological systems exhibiting self-organization

label: Continuum behavior emerges from discrete randomizing conserving rules
statement: Smooth continuum behavior, such as diffusion of density, emerges from discrete systems whenever small-scale apparent randomness washes out individual details and conserved quantities constrain overall features, as shown by block cellular automata whose average density follows the diffusion equation.
quote: And much as in physical systems like fluids, what ultimately leads to this is the presence of small-scale apparent randomness that washes out details of individual cells or molecules—as well as of conserved quantities that force certain overall features not to change too quickly.
scope: discrete systems with conserved quantities and intrinsic randomness, such as particle-conserving block cellular automata and fluids

label: A very simple program may underlie all of physics
statement: Underneath the known laws of physics there may be a single very simple program from which all known laws, and all the complexity of the universe, emerge.
quote: Underneath the laws of physics as we know them today it could be that there lies a very simple program from which all the known laws—and ultimately all the complexity we see in the universe—emerges.
scope: the fundamental laws of the universe

label: The fundamental rule cannot be found by working backwards from known laws
statement: If the ultimate rule for the universe is simple, it cannot realistically be found by engineering it from observed features; the only practical method is to choose a straightforward representation and systematically search through large numbers of candidate rules.
quote: my guess is that the only realistic way to find the rule in the first place will be to start from some very straightforward representation, and then just to search through large numbers of possible rules in this representation.
scope: methodology for finding a fundamental theory of physics

label: Most known physical laws are emergent, not fundamental
statement: Most physical laws discovered so far are not fundamental but are emergent large-scale features of an underlying rule, so their simplicity says little about the simplicity of that rule.
quote: I strongly suspect that the vast majority of physical laws discovered so far are not truly fundamental, but are instead merely emergent features of the large-scale behavior of some ultimate underlying rule.
scope: known laws of physics

label: Space, gravity and quantum features are generic across many candidate rules
statement: Features such as seemingly continuous space and certain aspects of gravitation and quantum mechanics will emerge from many different underlying rules for the universe, whereas properties like the spectrum of particle masses, and perhaps the dimensionality of space, will be specific to particular rules.
quote: so also I suspect that properties such as the existence of seemingly continuous space, as well as certain features of gravitation and quantum mechanics, will emerge with many different possible underlying rules for the universe.
scope: candidate fundamental rules for the universe

label: Space is discrete below the scales probed by experiment
statement: Space, though experimentally continuous down to about 10^-20 meters, is very likely made of discrete elements at still smaller scales, just as fluids and other seemingly continuous things have turned out to be.
quote: Particle physics experiments have shown that space acts as a continuum down to distances of around 10-20 meters—or a hundred thousandth the radius of a proton. But there is absolutely no reason to think that discrete elements will not be found at still smaller distances.
scope: the structure of physical space at very small distances

label: Space and matter should be made of the same stuff
statement: In the simplest ultimate model of the universe there is no distinction between space and its contents: matter and everything else are made of the same underlying structure as space, unlike in a cellular automaton.
quote: But if the ultimate model for the universe is to be as simple as possible, then it seems much more plausible that both space and its contents should somehow be made of the same stuff—so that in a sense space becomes the only thing in the universe.
scope: fundamental structure of space and matter

label: At the lowest level space is a network of nodes
statement: At the lowest level, space is most likely a giant network of nodes defined only by their connections (and it suffices to consider nodes with exactly three connections), with ordinary space emerging as a large-scale limit.
quote: And with this in mind I believe that what is by far the most likely is that at the lowest level space is in effect a giant network of nodes.
scope: fundamental structure of physical space

label: Network dimension is set by growth of node counts with distance
statement: A network corresponds to ordinary d-dimensional space exactly when the number of nodes within graph distance r of a node grows in a limiting sense like r^d; tree-like or randomly connected networks correspond to no finite dimension.
quote: in general the condition for a network to correspond to ordinary d-dimensional space is precisely that the total number of nodes that appear in it out to distance r grows in some limiting sense like rd
scope: large networks and their correspondence to finite-dimensional space

label: Observers perceive time only through the causal network of events
statement: An observer embedded in a system such as a mobile automaton cannot see its individual update steps; all the observer can perceive is the network of causal relationships between updating events, so perceived time and spacetime derive purely from that causal network, and sequential updating can appear as synchronized parallel evolution.
quote: The most they will be able to tell is that a certain network of causal relationships exists—and their perception of time must therefore derive purely from the properties of this network.
scope: observers embedded in discrete evolving systems, including the universe

label: Non-overlapping replacement rules give update-order-independent causal networks
statement: A substitution system whose rules replace only blocks that can never overlap themselves or each other always yields the same causal network regardless of the order in which replacements are applied (the property Wolfram calls causal invariance).
quote: And any substitution system whose rules specify replacements only for blocks such as these is guaranteed to yield the same causal network regardless of the order in which replacements are performed.
scope: string substitution systems and, analogously, network rewriting systems

label: The universe's rules likely yield a unique causal network
statement: Although the universe has no global clock and its rules may be applicable in arbitrary order, its actual rules most likely have the property of always yielding the same causal network, and so a unique perceived history.
quote: it still tends to be my suspicion that there is not—and that in fact the particular rules followed by the universe do in the end have the property that they always yield the same causal network.
scope: the fundamental update rules of the universe

label: Small-scale randomness in the network makes space robustly 3D
statement: The ultimate rules for the universe will produce networks that look largely random at small scales, and this randomness is what allows a definite and robust dimensionality of 3 to emerge for space.
quote: my expectation is that they will give rise to networks that on a small scale look largely random. But this very randomness will most likely be what for example allows a definite and robust value of 3 to emerge for the dimensionality of space
scope: network models of space and the dimensionality of physical space

label: Elementary length and time are tiny and their ratio is light speed
statement: Each connection in the causal network of the universe corresponds to an identical elementary distance (perhaps about 10^-35 meters) and elementary time (perhaps about 10^-43 seconds), whose ratio is a fixed speed identified with the speed of light.
quote: One may guess that this elementary distance is around 10-35 meters, and that the elementary time interval is around 10-43 seconds. But whatever these values are, a crucial point is that their ratio must be a fixed speed, and we can identify this with the speed of light.
scope: discrete structure of spacetime

label: Causal invariance yields special relativity
statement: If the underlying rules of the universe are causal invariant, then slices through the causal network at different angles, corresponding to different uniform velocities, are all governed by the same rules, so physics is the same regardless of uniform motion and the standard phenomena of special relativity such as time dilation follow.
quote: And the crucial point is that whenever the underlying system is causal invariant the exact same underlying rules will account for what one sees in slices at different angles. And what this means is that in effect the same rules will apply regardless of how fast one is going.
scope: discrete causal network models of spacetime and special relativity

label: Elementary particles are persistent localized structures in the network
statement: Elementary particles are analogs of the localized structures seen in class 4 cellular automata: persistent structures (such as tangles or non-planar cores) in the network of space, so that the fundamental rules need make no reference to particular particles.
quote: An immediate possibility that I suspect is actually not too far from the mark is that such particles are analogs of the localized structures that we saw earlier in this book in systems like the class 4 cellular automata shown below.
scope: elementary particles of physics

label: Fundamental particle masses may still have simple ratios
statement: Although observed elementary particle masses are not in simple ratios (unlike electric charges), truly fundamental particle masses may still have simple relations, because observed masses include varying amounts of interaction energy.
quote: But despite such results, it is still conceivable that there could in the end be simple relations between truly fundamental particle masses—since it turns out that the masses that have actually been observed in effect also include varying amounts of interaction energy.
scope: masses of elementary particles such as leptons and quarks
